book:when-god-bless-america-replaces-thy.title: When God Bless America Replaces Thy Kingdom Come
book:when-god-bless-america-replaces-thy.notes: Calm and unhyped, but the one sentence after the subtitle merely restates it: "How Patriotism Became Our Practical Savior" is followed by "how patriotism has replaced the kingdom of God as the practical savior," so "practical savior" lands twice in thirty words and the reader learns nothing the title did not say. "A direct examination" is catalog labeling, not a thought. Replace the sentence with the book's actual claim (what was traded, who did the trading, that the writer is inside it) and it ships.

book:the-monster-in-the-mirror.title: The Monster in the Mirror
book:the-monster-in-the-mirror.notes: The subtitle carries the self-implication ("Why Yours Is No Different"); the blurb sentence drops it and retreats to inert catalog copy: "An exploration of how each generation interprets Scripture through its own cultural lens." No hype, nothing forbidden, but "exploration" and "cultural lens" could describe any hermeneutics primer. Rewrite the sentence so the mirror turns on the reader and the writer, which is the book's whole point.

book:pcn-healthy-growing-church.title: The Healthy & Growing Church
book:pcn-healthy-growing-church.notes: The blurb is a keyword string, not a sentence with a thought: "Comprehensive guide on church health, decline, revitalization, replanting, and leading without losing hope." "Comprehensive guide" is a promise no book keeps, and the subtitle's "Breaking Through the Plateau" reads as church-growth-conference language. The one human phrase, "leading without losing hope," is the seed of a real blurb; build from that and drop the inventory.

book:pcn-patient-pastor.title: The Patient Pastor
book:pcn-patient-pastor.notes: "Master the skill of patient leadership and strategic change management" is an imperative brochure hook in corporate-church language; "master the skill" is a promise, and "strategic change management" is the business-seminar vocabulary the voice standard names as corporate church language. Nothing here sounds like a pastor speaking across a table. The subtitle ("Without Losing Your Church or Your Mind") is the honest line; the blurb should grow from it.

book:pcn-change-without-casualties.title: Change Without Casualties
book:pcn-change-without-casualties.notes: "Strategic guide for implementing change while maintaining congregational trust" is management copy: "strategic," "implementing," "maintaining" are the words of a consultant's deck, not a pastor who has watched a church split over a decision. The title's real weight (casualties, meaning people) is absent from the blurb. Rebuild around the cost the title names.

book:pcn-changing-unchangeable.title: Changing the Unchangeable
book:pcn-changing-unchangeable.notes: "Face institutional resistance and lead real change in traditional churches" is a conference-session imperative, the artificially dramatic hook the standard tells us to avoid, and "lead real change" is generic leadership copy. The subtitle's "We've Always Done It This Way" is a genuine, spoken line; the blurb should sound like the man who has heard it in a deacons' meeting, with the fairness to say why people say it before challenging them.

book:livewell-staying.title: Staying
book:livewell-staying.notes: The subtitle ("Depression, Crisis, and the Long Middle") is the most honest copy in the set; the sentence under it softens into publishing stock: "life's most difficult seasons" and "with honesty and grace" are the filler phrases of a hundred Christian marriage books. Nothing validates despair or diagnoses the reader, so the care is intact, but a blurb that names depression should let the book's page keep a visible path to real help beside it. Replace the two stock phrases with what the book actually says about staying when staying is hard.

book:dangerous-calling-why-the-office-of.title: Dangerous Calling: Why the Office of Pastor Is Not for Everyone
book:dangerous-calling-why-the-office-of.notes: Three stock jacket sentences: the book labels itself "A prophetic examination" (prophetic is something a book is, not something it announces), "what it truly means to be called" is filler, "both the glory and the weight" is perfect symmetry, and "Essential reading for anyone" is the hype closer. The claim about "the romanticization of ministry" is real and specific; keep it and cut the rest. Separately, a human should rule on the title: Paul David Tripp published Dangerous Calling (Crossway, 2012) on the same subject, and the blurb does nothing to distinguish this book from it.

book:the-hidden-life-of-a-pastor-tending.title: The Hidden Life of a Pastor: Tending Your Soul While Tending the Flock
book:the-hidden-life-of-a-pastor-tending.notes: Pure template with no sentence that could only be about this book: "A pastoral guide to spiritual formation and personal renewal," a list ("their struggles, temptations, and spiritual disciplines"), then "a companion to pastoral leaders seeking to maintain their own spiritual vitality," which is corporate-church vocabulary. It is burnout-adjacent copy and nothing in it validates despair, but it also honors no real pain; it gestures at "struggles" without naming one. Rebuild from the subtitle's actual tension: the soul that goes untended while the flock is tended.

stockPhrases: A pastoral guide to spiritual formation and personal renewal

book:the-first-flock-the-church-s-callin.title: The First Flock: The Church's Calling to Care for Pastors and Their Families
book:the-first-flock-the-church-s-callin.notes: The thesis sentence states the book's argument backwards: "Bell argues that the congregation is the pastors \"first flock\", they must be cared for with the same intentionality as the broader church." The subtitle says the church is called to care for pastors and their families, so the pastor's household, not the congregation, is the first flock; as written the blurb misleads the buyer about what the book claims. It is also a comma splice with a missing apostrophe and straight quotes, and "with the same intentionality" is corporate filler. The last sentence ("from taking pastors for granted to actively supporting them") is the only usable line.

book:earthen-vessels-why-our-bodies-matt.title: Earthen Vessels: Why Our Bodies Matter to Our Faith
book:earthen-vessels-why-our-bodies-matt.notes: The middle sentence carries a real position ("challenges the dualism that separates spirit from body"), and "whole Christianity that honors the physical" stays just this side of holistic. The failures are surface: "A theological exploration of" is the template opener and "incarnational living" is insider church jargon that explains nothing to the skeptic. Beyond the copy, a human must rule on the title: Matthew Lee Anderson published Earthen Vessels: Why Our Bodies Matter to Our Faith (Bethany House, 2011), the identical title and subtitle, and the site's integrity claim cannot carry that unexamined.

book:preach-the-word-the-primacy-of-expo.title: Preach the Word: The Primacy of Expository Preaching in the Local Church
book:preach-the-word-the-primacy-of-expo.notes: "This book is essential for preachers" is the hype closer, and "practical concerns about relevance and engagement" is conference-track vocabulary. The middle claim ("makes the case for text-driven preaching") is real but generic; the voice standard asks for fairness before sharpness, so the blurb should say plainly what the strongest case against expository preaching is before saying the book answers it. Cut the closer and it is close.

book:the-undershepherd-pastoral-leadersh.title: The Undershepherd: Pastoral Leadership, Authority, and the Care of God's People
book:the-undershepherd-pastoral-leadersh.notes: "A comprehensive theology of pastoral leadership" promises what no single book delivers; drop "comprehensive." The middle sentence is the honest core (under-shepherd accountable to Christ the Chief Shepherd, which is 1 Peter 5 without saying so) and should stay. Two missing apostrophes ("the pastors role," "the pastors responsibility") need fixing, and the closing list ("authority, care, discipline") is a table of contents rather than a thought.

book:the-pruning-church-decline-faithful.title: The Pruning: Church Decline, Faithful Endurance, and the Promise of Renewal
book:the-pruning-church-decline-faithful.notes: The thesis sentence makes the exact move the voice standard forbids, attaching generic hope to an unresolved diagnosis: "see decline not as failure but as opportunity for renewal and refocus." "Opportunity" is corporate, and a church watching its people die deserves better than a reframe. "A prophetic word" is self-labeling, "offers hope and practical guidance" and "seasons of loss and transition" are stock. The John 15 image of pruning is strong enough to build a real blurb from, if the blurb is willing to say that pruning cuts.

stockPhrases: not as failure but as opportunity

book:one-body-many-churches-a-theology-o.title: One Body, Many Churches: A Theology of Unity for a Fractured Church
book:one-body-many-churches-a-theology-o.notes: The middle sentence states a real position ("a robust doctrine of the universal church while honoring local church distinctives"), though "robust" is the reflexive adjective of seminary marketing and can go. "A theological exploration of" opens the same template as a dozen other blurbs here, and "This book addresses fragmentation, cooperation, and the church's witness" is a topic list. Name one fracture the book actually takes on and the blurb earns its title.

book:necessary-words-a-pastoral-theology.title: Necessary Words: A Pastoral Theology of Courage and Difficult Conversations
book:necessary-words-a-pastoral-theology.notes: "This book equips leaders with biblical wisdom" is church-conference copy, and "speaking truth in love" uses Ephesians 4:15 as a stock phrase rather than a quoted text. The middle sentence names real work ("confronting sin, addressing conflict, and speaking difficult truths") and "conversations that build rather than destroy" is a fair line. Fix the missing apostrophe in "the pastors prophetic role," cut "equips," and let the blurb admit what these conversations cost the one who has them.

book:sent-into-the-city-the-church-s-cal.title: Sent Into the City: The Church's Calling to Its Neighborhood and World
book:sent-into-the-city-the-church-s-cal.notes: Nearly every noun phrase is a conference track title: "missional engagement," "community involvement," "social justice, community transformation, and kingdom witness." "Community transformation" is the forbidden word's cousin, and the stack of jargon is what the voice standard calls corporate church language. The one real line, "move beyond programs to genuine presence in their neighborhoods," should be the whole blurb's spine, stated in plain words a neighbor could read.

book:to-the-ends-of-the-earth-global-mis.title: To the Ends of the Earth: Global Mission, National Partnership, and the Sent Church
book:to-the-ends-of-the-earth-global-mis.notes: No sentence here is about this book rather than any missions book: "explores the church's role in world missions, cross-cultural partnership, and the global nature of God's kingdom" is a topic list, and "calls the church to think globally" is half a bumper sticker. The subtitle's "National Partnership" implies a specific argument about partnering with national leaders rather than exporting Western ministry, and the blurb never says it. Build the blurb on that claim.

book:faithful-in-exile-pastoral-leadersh.title: Faithful in Exile: Pastoral Leadership and the Church's Witness in a Post-Christian Age
book:faithful-in-exile-pastoral-leadersh.notes: Empty template from first word to last: "A prophetic guide" self-labels, "maintain faithfulness and witness in a post-Christian context" is institutional vocabulary, and "offers both challenge and encouragement for leaders facing cultural change" is the symmetrical filler the standard names as sounding generated. The exile image (Jeremiah 29, 1 Peter) is the strongest thing the title has and the blurb never touches it. Rebuild from the image and say what faithfulness costs when the culture has stopped listening.

book:common-grace-what-pastors-learn-whe.title: Common Grace: What Pastors Learn When They Listen to the World
book:common-grace-what-pastors-learn-whe.notes: The middle sentence is a real, slightly surprising claim ("pastors must listen to the world to understand God's common grace at work") and matches the subtitle; keep it. The frame around it is template: "A theology of common grace and cultural engagement" and "calls for thoughtful engagement" use "engagement" twice in three sentences, and "challenges Christian isolation" points at others without the self-implication the man would supply. Cut the repetition and let the blurb concede what the isolated church is afraid of.

book:the-unfinished-church-calling-visio.title: The Unfinished Church: Calling, Vision, and the Future God Is Building
book:the-unfinished-church-calling-visio.notes: Hollow throughout: "A vision for the church's future and God's ongoing work," "the church's road" (which reads as journey-as-metaphor with the word swapped and the metaphor left standing), "God's unfolding story," and "offers hope and direction" are generic Christian inspiration, and "future" appears three times in three sentences. Nothing states what the book argues or what is unfinished. Rebuild from a concrete claim, or the blurb tells the buyer this is a book about nothing in particular.

stockPhrases: A vision for the church's future

Two facts to verify rather than voice failures: "nearly eighteen thousand pastors" / "nearly 18,000" sits beside CLAUDE.md's vaguer "thousands", and "twelve years" at FBC Fenton appears as a literal while the closing uses SITE_STATS.yearsInMinistryWord, so the two numbers can drift apart on the same page. Em-dashes in blocks 28 and 29 are within the sparing allowance.

The opening line earns its place: "A platform that writes about reaching the excluded has no business excluding anyone at the door." The fragment run in "What is in place" is a genuine inventory, not prose fractured into bullets, and "A person reads that inbox" is exactly the right register for the ask.

The fragment triplet ("The catechism that began with why. The eleven chapters of Romans before the first command. The grace that came before the law at Sinai.") sits at a genuine hinge and can stay.

page:client/src/pages/books/WhyNotWhatTh.notes: No reader-facing prose in this file; the only text is a code comment and the page delegates to the shared EbookThankYou component. Nothing to audit here — the thank-you copy should be audited where it lives.

page:client/src/pages/comparisons/Baptis.notes: Voice is right: fair columns, a real hero ("One insists you choose your own baptism. The other says grace got there first."), and an earned close ("The wrong answer is the one you hold because you have never considered the alternative."). Two facts need tightening: "The United Methodist Church formally split in 2023-2024" — the Global Methodist Church launched in May 2022 and disaffiliations ran 2019–2023, so the date range is off; and "African and Asian Methodists, who are theologically conservative and numerically dominant in the global denomination" overstates a contested membership picture. "The splits are not signs of weakness. They are signs that the questions still matter" reads a little glib about schism next to the platform's own grief over division elsewhere.

page:client/src/pages/comparisons/Calvin.notes: Strong steelmans on both columns, the intramural framing ("The argument is inside the family"), and a verdict that lands ("A theology that accounts for only one of them is not a theology. It is an editorial decision."). One factual slip: "Calvin never used the TULIP acronym — that was a later systematization from the Synod of Dort" conflates the five points (Dort, 1618–19) with the acronym, which is an early-twentieth-century mnemonic; say the points come from Dort and the acronym came centuries later.

page:client/src/pages/comparisons/Cathol.notes: The hero is a stacked antithesis with em-dashes doing the connecting — "Not because the differences are trivial — because they are not. And not because reconciliation is impossible — because the shared ground runs deeper" — exactly the "not this but that" gait the voice standard retires; rewrite it as two plain sentences. The body is fair ("Neither column is a caricature"), the FAQ on closed communion and Marian veneration steelmans well, and "The worst thing either side can do is caricature the other. And both sides do it constantly" is a real verdict. "Council of Trent, 1545" should read 1545–1563 (the justification decree is 1547).

page:client/src/pages/comparisons/Evange.notes: The page leans on perfect symmetry the standard warns against — "Evangelicalism without mainline social conscience becomes theologically rigorous and socially blind. Mainline Protestantism without evangelical conviction becomes socially relevant and theologically empty" — and the hero ("Both are right about the other's blind spot") sets that pattern; loosen the parallelism where the evidence is not symmetrical. Two source problems: "The Dorothy Day model" is offered as the mainline mission archetype, but Day was Catholic; and the Pennsylvania Railroad origin of "mainline" is stated flat ("these were the churches on the main line of the Pennsylvania Railroad") when it is a popular, disputed etymology. "Theological diversity within a tradition is a feature, not a bug" is a tech cliché.

page:client/src/pages/comparisons/Liturg.notes: Fair columns, a good hero ("One tradition hands you a prayer book. The other hands you a setlist."), and the lex orandi answer is the best thing on the page. One citation cannot stand as written: "James K.A. Smith: liturgies are 'formative practices that train our hearts'" is presented in quotation marks and I cannot verify it as verbatim — either source it to the page in Desiring the Kingdom or drop the quotes and paraphrase ("Smith argues that liturgies are formative practices that train the heart"). "the first nineteen centuries of Christianity would not recognize it" is hyperbole doing the work a sentence of history should do.

page:client/src/pages/comparisons/Orthod.notes: The most fully realized of the comparison pages: both columns stated in their own voice (the filioque row lets each side make its case), the 1204 row keeps the wound visible ("It was Christians attacking Christians under the banner of the cross"), and the close is a verdict rather than a recap ("The division is a scandal. And the scandal is that both sides know it."). Minor: "Icons — two-dimensional depictions written (not painted)" repeats a popular claim about the Greek verb that specialists dispute; a softer "often described as 'written'" would be safer.

page:client/src/pages/faq/CanScienceAndF.notes: The register is calm and the history is mostly sound (Draper-White, Lemaitre, Penzias and Wilson, the 2009 Pew figure). Three claims need verification or softening: "The Venerable Bede, in the eighth century, accepted an allegorical reading" of the Genesis days is doubtful — Bede's Genesis commentary is largely literal; Einstein resisting the Big Bang "partly because it sounded too much like creation" is not the usual account of his objection; and the parenthetical that Hoyle coined the term "as a mockery" is contested by Hoyle himself. "a need driven by ideology, not by evidence" is sharper than the page has earned against the people it names.

page:client/src/pages/faq/DoesGodExist.t.notes: Written toward the skeptic as the standard asks — the objections get their strongest form ("These are serious objections, and the Christian who dismisses them has not understood them") and the suffering answer refuses a tidy theodicy ("Job's answer is not an explanation. It is an encounter."). One attribution is wrong: "The cosmological argument, refined by Leibniz and restated by William Lane Craig, observes that everything that begins to exist has a cause" — that is the kalam, not Leibniz's contingency argument; separate them. "The idea that faith requires absolute certainty is a modern evangelical invention" is a sweeping accusation without a named distinction, and "That is not credulity. That is courage." is a slogan where the paragraph had already made the point.

page:client/src/pages/faq/IsBibleHistori.notes: Honest on both fronts (the exodus and conquest conceded; contradictions named rather than harmonized), and the closing answer on reading honestly is good. The hero ends on a signpost hook, "Here is what we actually know," which is the stock turn the standard names. Two facts to fix: Hezekiah's tunnel "was discovered in 1838 with an inscription describing its construction" — the tunnel was surveyed in 1838, the Siloam inscription found in 1880; and "roughly 10 manuscripts of Caesar's Gallic Wars" is an outdated apologetics figure (the count runs into the hundreds; the ninth-century earliest date is the defensible point).

stockPhrases: Here is what we actually know.

page:client/src/pages/faq/WhatDenominati.notes: The pastoral counsel is the real thing — "Ask what the pastor has read recently. If the answer is only church leadership books, keep looking," and "A church that tells you the truth with tears in its eyes." The hero closes on the same stock hook as the sibling FAQs: "Here is what actually matters." Cut it and let "tribalism dressed as theology" carry the line. "Non-denominational churches start from scratch every generation" is a generalization the page does not support.

page:client/src/pages/faq/WhatDoChristia.notes: Handles a contested doctrine the way the Scholarship Standard requires: three positions in their strongest form, the historical diversity stated accurately (Gregory of Nyssa "was never condemned for his universalism"; 553 handled with the proper hedge), and the warnings kept pastoral ("they were given in tears, not triumph"). The final verdict carries weight without cruelty: "a loving God does something worse: he honors the choice."

page:client/src/pages/faq/WhatIsDeconstr.notes: Reconstruction, not demolition — the page does the second thing ("It does not look like going back. It looks like going through") and implicates the church ("When a seminary professor questions inerrancy, it is called scholarship. When a twenty-six-year-old in a megachurch does it, it is called falling away."). One unverifiable claim: "The Liturgists podcast, though now ended" — confirm its status or drop the clause. The wilderness stage is named honestly and therapy is pointed to for abuse cases, which keeps the help path visible.

page:client/src/pages/faq/WhatIsReligiou.notes: The care is right — real organizations named, therapy modalities described, grief legitimized, and leaving faith handled without coercion ("that is between them and God — not between them and the church that hurt them"). The voice fails the fair-before-sharp test in two places: the hero "The church caused this" is a blanket accusation with no named distinction between the systems described and the churches that did not do this; and the answer to whether religious trauma is real dismisses the honest questioner ("is usually asked by people who have never experienced it. For those who have, the question answers itself") instead of conceding what is fair in the question. "intention does not determine impact" is borrowed cliché.

page:client/src/pages/faq/WhatIsTheDiffe.notes: Substantively strong and even-handed — the Westminster "Antichrist" line is quoted honestly alongside its recognition of Catholic baptism, and the papacy answer ends well ("They are not questions that should prevent Christians from recognizing one another"). The hero closes on the stock hook "Here is what actually divides them." One category error: "most mainstream Protestant denominations -- including the World Council of Churches" — the WCC is a council, not a denomination.

stockPhrases: Here is what actually divides them.

page:client/src/pages/faq/WhyArePeopleLe.notes: The Jeremiah close is the platform's voice at its best ("The judgment was on what Israel had made of God's house. The mercy was that God was not finished.") and the hero is self-implicating. The numbers contradict each other: one answer says "The Southern Baptist Convention has lost roughly 1.3 million members since 2006" while the next says it "peaked at 16.3 million members in 2006 and has fallen to roughly 13 million" — that is a loss of over three million; reconcile. "only 36% of Millennials (born 1981-1996) identify as Protestant or Catholic, compared to 67% of the Silent Generation" does not match the Pew figures I know and needs a source. "a culture that prizes individual authenticity" trips the forbidden list in noun form; "self-expression" or Taylor's own "the age of authenticity" in quotes would be cleaner.

page:client/src/pages/faq/WhyDoYoungPeop.notes: Good diagnostic spine ("The church lost them not by asking too much but by offering too little"; "The young just leave first") and it refuses one-directional politics. Verify the claim that a "2022 survey by the Survey Center on American Life found that the single most common reason young adults gave for leaving their childhood religion was that it became too focused on politics" — my recollection is that ceasing to believe the teachings ranked first, with politics lower. "unlocking keychain leadership" is Fuller's own commitment name, but it is unmarked as a quotation and lands a forbidden word in the site's voice; put the phrase in quotes and attribute it. "The Silent Generation produced the sexual revolution" is contestable generational shorthand.

page:client/src/pages/history/HistoryEss.notes: A rendering shell with no authored copy — title, subtitle, sections, figures, and sources all come from the JSON essay files. Nothing here to audit; the prose must be judged in the library it loads.

page:client/src/pages/landing/ChurchHist.notes: Calm, declarative, historically anchored (313, 380, 1517) and correct on each date. The FAQ answers steelman all three traditions ("Each tradition carries real wisdom and real blind spots") and the Christendom answer draws the named distinction the standard asks for ("If you mean the Christendom model... yes, that is over. If you mean a living faith that costs something... the story is more complicated"). The signup fragments ("Where it came from. What went wrong. What still holds.") are acceptable at blurb length.

page:client/src/pages/landing/ChurchHurt.notes: The care standard is met: 988 is named at the top, external organizations are listed, forgiveness is not pressed ("They do not ask you to forgive on someone else's timeline"), and the door back to church is left open without pressure. Two copy fixes: the description doubles itself ("...and the long road back. Essays on spiritual abuse, religious trauma, purity culture, and the long road to healing.") — keep one; and "give yourself permission to heal" / "it takes permission to be angry" drift into counseling idiom the voice standard avoids — say the same thing plainly (anger is allowed; no one gets to set your timeline). The hero's "naming it is the first step toward healing" is close to the same register; consider ending on "was not God."

page:client/src/pages/landing/Deconstruc.notes: The hero and byline are right ("the questions that scare the church are the same ones that make faith real"), the Great Dechurching and Pew citations are real, and the FAQs are pastoral. Copy failures: "does not require them to check their brain at the door" and "circle the wagons" are stock idioms; the signup blurb "No guilt. No conversion bait. Just honest theology." is a marketing fragment stack. Unlike its sibling FaithCrisis page, this doubt-facing landing offers no path to real help at all — a short pointer to a person, not only a reading list, belongs here.

stockPhrases: check their brain at the door
No guilt. No conversion bait. Just honest theology.

page:client/src/pages/landing/FaithCrisi.notes: The model for a crisis-facing page: it honors the feeling without validating despair ("Doubt is not an emergency. But it rarely travels alone — and if what came with it is despair... that part deserves a real person, not just a reading list"), names 988 and licensed therapy plainly, and promises company rather than resolution ("They offer company for the long road."). The hero carries weight in one line.

page:client/src/pages/landing/Grief.tsx.notes: Every line earns its place: "Grief is the evidence that you loved something real" and "These essays sit in the wreckage with you, not above it" honor the pain without a fix. The help section is exactly the care standard: "Writing can keep you company. It cannot sit across a table from you," then 988, GriefShare, and counselors, with "not wanting to be here" named as "a today conversation, not a someday one." The only tic is the "Not platitudes." fragment in the Prayer Generator blurb, too small to hold the page.

page:client/src/pages/landing/HonestQues.notes: The FAQ answers are the real thing ("If God cannot handle your questions, God is not God"; "a God who enters suffering rather than explaining it away. That is not a complete answer. It is the beginning of one"). The page-furniture around them slips into ad copy: the "No X. No Y. Just Z." formula runs twice ("No cliches. No bait-and-switch. Just honest engagement"; "No guilt. No pressure. Just theology that takes your intelligence seriously") and the meta line "answered without flinching" is a hype hook. Also check "asked every one of these questions before he believed a word of the gospel": the former-atheist fact is real, the "every one of these questions" claim is an extension James should confirm.

stockPhrases: No cliches. No bait-and-switch. Just honest engagement
No guilt. No pressure. Just theology that takes your intelligence seriously

page:client/src/pages/landing/MarriageCr.notes: The help section is the best on the site: it names abuse as "not a marriage problem to work through. It is a safety question, and it is a today conversation," and the hotline line "for you even if you are only wondering whether it counts" is real care. The problem is the stats copy above it: "Marriage does not fail because two people are incompatible. It fails because two people stop doing the costly work of seeing each other" is a universal cause that the page's own abuse paragraph refutes, and a spouse whose marriage ended by the other's abandonment or violence reads it as a verdict on them. Qualify it so the blame is not automatically shared. Minor: the book blurb ("Before you lead a church, you lead a family") is pitched at pastors on a page for anyone.

page:client/src/pages/landing/ParentingS.notes: The FAQ answers are the mature register in full paragraphs: "Believe the injury first. The God who was misrepresented to them is not the same as the room where it happened, but they will only hear that after they have been heard." The Deuteronomy 6 material is offered as paraphrase, not quotation, and is accurate. The help section keeps 988, counselors, and "If you have a pastor, call them tonight" visible without diagnosing anyone. One small tic to trim when convenient: the Parenting Guide blurb's "Not rules. Not shame. Just honest direction."

stockPhrases: Not rules. Not shame. Just honest direction.

page:client/src/pages/landing/PastoralBu.notes: "The weight you carry is real. The exhaustion is not weakness. And the silence around it is not safety" honors the pain and names the mechanism without therapy language. The help section refuses to let the essays pose as care ("Essays help a pastor feel less alone. They are not care") and ends on a line that carries weight: "asking for help is not the end of your ministry. It is usually how it survives." "Pastors call it too" on the 988 card is exactly right. "written from inside the room, not from a safe distance" is the positioning statement reused verbatim across several landing pages; not a failure, but it is becoming a house phrase.

page:client/src/pages/landing/PostChrist.notes: The argument block has a real thesis ("Christianity is not dying. Something is dying"), but the surrounding copy sells rather than states: "Sixty essays. Seven tiers. The full story of how the most powerful religious movement in Western history is losing its grip" is a fragment stack plus an overclaim, the anaphora triplet "Written by a pastor. Written from inside the room. Written for anyone who refuses to settle for easy answers in either direction" is exactly the generated-sounding symmetry the standard names, and "No spam. No guilt" is newsletter boilerplate. "may be closer to the original thing than anything Christendom ever produced" is a large historical verdict delivered as hero copy with no argument under it; either earn it or soften it. Confirm the series actually contains sixty live essays before the number stays.

stockPhrases: Sixty essays. Seven tiers. The full story
Written by a pastor. Written from inside the room. Written for anyone who
refuses to settle for easy answers in either direction

page:client/src/pages/leadership/BeforeY.notes: "A leader can lose in thirty seconds online what took thirty years to build. This is not a content filter. It is a heart filter" is a single antithesis at the hinge, then plain instruction. The results copy refuses false comfort: "Nothing here flagged. That does not make it wise, only clear of the obvious traps. Say it plainly, say it once, and be willing to own it in the morning." Calm, declarative, and it ends on the reader's responsibility rather than a recap.

page:client/src/pages/leadership/BudgetC.notes: The voice is right ("Show a church its budget and it will tell you what that church actually worships"; "A church with no reserve is one furnace away from a crisis"). Two claims need grounding or removal: "The ranges are guides drawn from healthy churches" asserts an empirical source that is never named, and on a money tool the CLAUDE.md care standard asks for a plain "this is not financial advice" line, which "not commandments" does not supply. Name where the ranges come from or drop "drawn from healthy churches"; add the one-line disclaimer.

page:client/src/pages/leadership/Decisio.notes: "A church forgets its own decisions and then relitigates them. Keep the record" is the whole case in two sentences, and the privacy line ("This stays on your device. No name or figure is sent anywhere") is stated plainly rather than as reassurance. Nothing to fix.

page:client/src/pages/leadership/Formati.notes: Index copy is compressed and concrete: "character before competence, every session anchored in a text and a practice. Run them with an elder team, a cohort, or one man across a coffee table." The partial-guide notice ("More sessions in this guide are being written") is honest rather than promotional. Session content itself is JSON data and outside this extract.

The intro states the platform's thesis without hype ("The church's leadership catastrophes are almost entirely failures of formation, not skill") and then discloses the method as a list inside a sentence, which is fair for an index. "Each topic is labeled honestly: a biblical command, a contested conviction, or a prudential wisdom matter. You should know which one you are reading" is the triage discipline made visible to the reader. "the questions you answer at midnight, not the ones you answer in interviews" lands. "the best scholarship" is a small self-compliment that could go.

The domain readings are the mature register in full paragraphs, pastoral and precise: "It is a theology problem wearing a calendar costume"; "This is not a moral failure. It is what happens to almost everyone who is good at something people praise. But it cannot hold."; "You rest first, badly, restless and checking your phone, and the belief follows the practice." Verdicts carry weight ("You are gifted enough to outrun your character. Most leaders who fell were"; "Every public collapse you have watched began as a private one nobody inventoried"). The privacy and anti-oracle copy ("It is arithmetic on your own answers... Open a domain and check the work") is honest about what the tool is. Minor: "the slow work" recurs three times across intro, results, and trend copy.

The extract carries almost no prose; the shell copy that exists is the triage labels ("Scripture speaks directly. This is not a matter of style." / "Faithful Christians genuinely differ. Every view here is given its strongest voice." / "An open skill matter. Scripture gives principles, not a blueprint.") and "That topic is not here yet." All plain and correct. Topic bodies are JSON and outside this audit.

page:client/src/pages/leadership/Governa.notes: "The policies a church hopes it never needs" is the right subtitle, and the meta line carries the legal care standard in plain words: "Starting points, not legal advice." The policy bodies are data; the shell copy is clean.

page:client/src/pages/leadership/GuidedW.notes: Only functional copy survives the extract ("The answers you wrote here are still saved on this device. You can take a copy with you now"; "Twelve copies is the limit — delete one to save another"), and it is direct and honest about failure states. Workflow prompts live in JSON.

page:client/src/pages/leadership/Illustr.notes: "An illustration is a window that lets light onto the text. Every entry here names the point it serves, so you use it for the truth and not the applause" is a real homiletical conviction in two sentences, then plain instruction. "Nothing matches that yet" is the right empty state.

page:client/src/pages/leadership/LeaderA.notes: Shell copy only: "Picked up where you left off," "See where this leaves you," "What this suggests," "Change my answers," and the storage-failure line. Restrained and accurate; "What this suggests" rather than "Your score" keeps the instrument from posing as a verdict. Question sets and bands are JSON.

page:client/src/pages/leadership/Leaders.notes: Shell copy only ("That article is not here yet," "Further reading," "Keep reading," "Search the Leadership Library"). Nothing to correct; article bodies are JSON.

"Most of the job is not the part anyone applauds. It is the hospital room, the budget meeting, the volunteer who quit, the sermon due in four days, the elder who will not be moved" is concrete and pastoral; the fragment run that follows is a genuine list of the library's sections, not argument broken into pieces. The closing carries weight without recap: "The question is not whether you can build a crowd. It is whether you can be faithful in a place over time." One thing for James to rule on rather than a copy failure: the hub says "the people who carry a church" in the intro and "the men who carry a church" in the booklets section; the platform treats gender and office as a second-order question, so the inconsistency should be a decision, not an accident.

"Everything written here for the people who carry a church. Formation, leadership, preaching, and the careful handling of the text. Search it, or work through a category" says what the page is and stops. The meta's "Plain, serious, useful" describes the register and meets it.

page:client/src/pages/leadership/Meeting.notes: "Most church meetings are bad because no one decided what they were for. Start from a template, cut what does not belong, and give every item a time and an owner" is diagnosis then instruction in the church-communication register the standard calls for. "ends in decisions, not fog" is one earned antithesis.

page:client/src/pages/leadership/Profile.notes: Both result readings refuse the scorecard posture honestly: "The point is not a grade. It is to show you where the work is" and "A test like this points, it does not pronounce. The body confirms a gift over time, in the using of it." The second is a genuinely theological line about gifts, delivered in plain speech.

page:client/src/pages/leadership/SermonS.notes: "Series to preach straight through a book, and series gathered around a question a congregation is actually asking... A starting point, not a script" describes the tool accurately and keeps the preacher's own labor in view. Nothing to fix; the series bodies are JSON.

page:client/src/pages/leadership/SermonW.notes: Compressed, functional, calm: "Live in the text before you reach for a point. Find the one thing it is doing." The stage prompts are the best copy here ("Read it ten times before you read anyone on it," "Leave weight. Do not tie it in a bow."). One thing to thin if the file is touched again: four help lines lean on the same antithesis ("Not three things. One." / "Not a forced add-on. The real line." / "Not generic application. This room, this week."), which the governing standard lists as a tic once its work is done. Ships as it stands.

page:client/src/pages/leadership/Servant.notes: The hero is in register and self-implicating ("We assumed the basin and platformed the gift, and then acted surprised when the men we elevated could not carry the weight"). The failure is slogan density and repetition: the thesis line "He is not built in the spotlight. He is built in the years no one was watching" is printed twice on the page (thesis band and QUOTES block), "We assumed the basin and platformed the gift" is also printed twice, and mark 2's verdict "Character is the only credential that lasts" sits a screen above the closer "Character is the only competence that lasts." The QUOTES block is a stack of four aphorisms where the standard asks for one verdict earned by the argument. Dedupe and cut the quote stack to one line; the marks themselves can stay.

Free, and written to be used." Says what the book is and stops. The chapter bodies come from JSON and were not in this batch.

page:client/src/pages/leadership/Service.notes: The component carries only UI strings ("Couldn't save to this browser — your work here will not survive a reload," "Twelve copies is the limit — delete one to save another," "Saves stay in this browser"), all honest and calm. Who is in the hospital, who just lost someone, who has not been seen in a month." is exactly the compressed register: pastoral, specific, no hype. The privacy line ("Nothing about your people is sent anywhere") is a real promise stated plainly. The empty state "Add the people on your heart" is ordinary pastoral idiom, not filler. Ships.

page:client/src/pages/leadership/WholeBi.notes: Hero is declarative and earns its claims: I checked "every one with a full expository series" and "More than five hundred sermons" against content/archive/leadership-lib/whole-bible-sermons.json (66 books, 66 series, 586 sermons, no empty arcs), so the copy is true, and the in-page fallback "The full preaching arc for {book} is being written" is honest if a book ever lacks one. "Free, for the men who carry the weight of the pulpit" is a position, not a voice fault. The generated fallback line "every command exposing our need for the one who kept it for us" is in register.

page:client/src/pages/life/LifeDomain.ts.notes: Shell only: "That page is not here yet. It may have moved. Start from the Integrated Life index," plus section labels ("What it gets right," "Tested against Scripture," "Part n of 8"). Nothing to fault. page:client/src/pages/life/LifeIndex.tsx.notes: "The modern person lives in boxes. Faith in one, work in another, the body in another, money in a fourth that nobody opens in church. page:client/src/pages/nation/NationEssay.notes: Shell plus two default read-next blurbs ("The flagship. page:client/src/pages/nation/NationHub.t.notes: The hero argument is right and the statement band is a real verdict ("the danger is never only the other side — it is how badly we want our own to be"). page:client/src/pages/nation/NationPolic.notes: Component copy is labels and a headline ("If we actually had a biblical government." / "What it was." / "The principle." / "In America today, it might look like" / "The catch."), all calm and clear. page:client/src/pages/nation/NationScore.notes: One honesty problem in one sentence. The tally caption reads "However it splits, read it as the verdict it is meant to be," and the hub card for this tool says "The tally is meant to come out split." A page billed as "An even-handed measure" cannot also tell the reader its result was decided before the themes were scored; that is the symmetrical-criticism-by-design the standard warns against. Keep the true half ("No column adds up to the kingdom of God") and let the verdict be what the themes show, not what the tool was built to produce.

stockPhrases: read it as the verdict it is meant to be

page:client/src/pages/pillars/AfterChris.notes: The argument is in register and self-implicated ("I am not neutral here. I pastor a church that remembers when the culture did half its work"), and it distinguishes Christendom from Christianity fairly before the verdict. Two mechanical fixes: em-dashes are the standard connector here (five across three short paragraphs plus the blurbs), and two lines are cleverness for its own sake: "decided it would look good on a shield" and the Long Arc blurb "The church has ended before. It hasn't," which reads as a riddle rather than a claim. The triplet "out-lived, out-loved, and finally out-lasted" strains for its middle term.

stockPhrases: The church has ended before. It hasn't.

page:client/src/pages/pillars/CaptureByT.notes: Fair before sharp, exactly as the standard asks: it concedes the vocabulary is the Sermon on the Mount's and that "the church handed them over unused" before landing "The lord changes. The lordship does not." Self-implication is concrete without inventing biography ("a man who has flinched — who has softened a hard word because the room would have gone cold"). The statement line "It just dies quoting different verses" is an earned verdict. Em-dash count is on the high side but each one is doing work.

Gives the captured position its strongest form first ("It did not begin as betrayal. It began as gratitude — for a nation where the gospel could be preached without a permit, for grandfathers who bled on real beaches") and then implicates the writer without extending his biography beyond pastoring ("for years I did not ask which one they would obey first, because I was not sure of my own answer"). Dates are concrete (313, the 1950s). The ending passes through return rather than recap: "not with a party to leave but a Lord to return to." Ships.

page:client/src/pages/pillars/ReadingScr.notes: The opening is a genuine distinction stated fairly to both sides ("The right reads Romans 13 and skips Amos. The left reads Amos and skips Romans 1. Both call it just reading the text. Neither is lying."), and the self-implication is honest and un-invented ("I have preached the edited version. Most of us were discipled by it"). The statement "Scripture does not need rescuing. Our reading does" is the one earned verdict. Tool blurbs are plain and useful. Ships.

page:client/src/pages/pillars/ThePastora.notes: The voice is right and the pain is honored without being resolved. Two fixable problems. First, biography: "I have been on both sides of the counseling appointment" and "I have come apart quietly on Saturday nights and stood up anyway on Sunday mornings" are specific personal claims not among the facts the audit permits (atheism, no father, five sons, FBC Fenton); James must confirm them in his own words or the sentences come out. Second, this landing names doubt, burnout, grief, and a pastor who "could not get out of bed on Monday," then offers only self-scored instruments, one of them pitched on fear ("before the congregation finds out the hard way"); add one line pointing to a person or the Find Help page so the path to real help is visible on the page that names the crisis.

page:client/src/pages/plans/CarePlan.tsx.notes: The shell is calm and the care contract is kept: the JSON careNote renders and <CrisisHelp /> sits under every plan, so help stays visible. One line of sentimental filler to cut: the completion state "All eight weeks walked. Well done is an understatement" is fitness-app cheer, not this voice; "All eight weeks walked" alone carries the weight. page:client/src/pages/prophetic/Propheti.notes: "One standard, or two?" and "A mirror, not a weapon" set the posture correctly, and the tally feedback implicates the writer alongside the reader ("None of us reads this clean" / "One landed. That is enough to start"). Intro, note, tests, and closing render from consistency-check.json and were not in this batch.

"Many of these words have been turned into weapons. Here they are defined from the text and the tradition, with the loaded ones handled honestly from both sides" is a plain promise stated without heat, and the headline "The words, defined fairly" matches it. Definitions come from glossary.json and were not in this batch.

Section labels ("Read this first," "Worked one at a time," "In the writing") are quiet and honest about what is unfinished. Hero text, posture blurb, and topic intros come from the section config and were not in this batch.

The only authored copy is the SEO line, and it is in register: "The prophets indict, then lament, then promise. Words to grieve injustice, confess the church's own failure, and hope in the world God will set right." It names the church's failure before anyone else's. Sections and prayers render from JSON and were not in this batch.

The component carries no authored reader prose; every section body comes from methodology.json and the only literal string is "Loading…". Nothing here to fail. The methodology copy itself lives in the data file and is outside this unit.

It concedes both readers' suspicion before promising anything, and the "Where Christians differ" label keeps second-order questions open. "Here they are." is short but not a hook.

SEO line is calm and self-implicating in the right order: "injustices of history: those done in the name of Christ, of empire, of markets, of forced utopia. No system is the kingdom." The church is named first, before the outsiders. Intro and closing bodies come from data.

Only authored line: "The same sin, named on each side with equal candor. Movements and documented record, not private accusation." Equal candor is not the same as asserting equal blame, so it does not trip the voice standard's warning against forced symmetry. Rest is data-driven.
No authored prose reaches the reader from this component; the intro and witness bodies are fetched from witnesses.json. Nothing to assess here.

page:client/src/pages/resources/ContextG.notes: Pure renderer: title, subtitle, sections, key texts, sources, and related links all arrive from the guide JSON. No authored copy to audit.

page:client/src/pages/resources/ContextL.notes: This is the register the site wants. "Most of what we misread, we misread because we never noticed the distance" puts the writer inside the indictment; "To put you under the text as it actually stands, before our politics got to it" is fair before sharp; the closing "Context is not a weapon for winning arguments. It is a posture for losing them, to the text" is a verdict that carries weight rather than recapping. Ships as it stands.

Most of them are not" is a calm concession; "paid for at councils and sometimes at stakes" keeps the cost visible; "Read them slowly. They were written slowly" ends on weight. No hype, no recap.

page:client/src/pages/studyguides/StudyG.notes: Authored text is section labels only ("If the room goes quiet", "A scenario for the room", "Going deeper · for the hungry group", "This week, try this", "Open (read aloud)"). They are plain, spoken, and do their job; all body prose is data.

Practical resource register, correctly dialed down: "Each guide is a full toolkit for the person at the front of the room" and "Every guide is free, and the PDFs download right here" are functional, not hype. "Run a class on Sunday with no prep" is the one line that leans promotional; it is a claim the toolkit (script, primer, handout) can plausibly back, so it stays. Closing "More guides are on the way" is honest about scope.

page:client/src/pages/table/Table.tsx.notes: Substance is right ("The table was never ours to charge admission to" is a real verdict) but the mechanics fall into the older gait: em-dashes as the standard connector ("had no building — it met", "no license to buy — only", "walks them — but", "free to use — in your church", "— it exists to make you the host"), and the fragment stack "No stage. No expert required. One table, an open Bible, and someone willing to go first" is then repeated almost verbatim in the StatementBand two sections later. The SEO line "A one-place engine for making disciples" is corporate church language, and "In a country that has stopped coming to the sanctuary" is a sweeping claim stated as settled fact.

page:client/src/pages/table/TableStudy.t.notes: Only UI strings ("Back to The Table", "Loading the study…", "Rhythm."); all study prose is data. Nothing to fail.

page:client/src/pages/tools/BibleOnTopic.notes: Most framings are compressed Bell ("cleverness, which is folly that has learned to dress well"; "Scripture meets the anxious with presence, not a scolding"). Two fixes: the Friendship framing opens "Scripture knows you become the average of the people you keep close", which is the Jim Rohn self-help slogan passed off as what Scripture says; and the hero's "the heart of the passages worth knowing by heart" stumbles over its own repetition. Anxiety and suffering framings honor real pain without validating despair.

page:client/src/pages/tools/BibleReferen.notes: Overwhelmingly strong: fair before sharp on every passage, honest "How this gets misused" sections, real interpretive ranges. Three fixes. The anxiety topic asserts twice that "The Bible's most repeated command is 'Do not fear'" and "commands 'do not fear' more than 300 times", a circulating claim that cannot be verified as stated; per the standard it comes out or gets rewritten around the hole. The Sabbath takeaway ends "Resting is an act of faith that says 'God has this handled'", which is the forbidden "God's got this" in a thin disguise. The sexuality topic steelmans both readings and then declines to name where the author lands or what order of question it is, which the contested-doctrine protocol requires. Grief, suffering, and anxiety sections honor pain and name medication as not a failure of faith.

page:client/src/pages/tools/BibleStudy.t.notes: Book overviews are diagnostic and concrete ("Proverbs is wisdom literature, which means it trades in general truths, not absolute promises"; "you cannot understand who Jesus is until you see how He dies"), citations check out (Luther's "epistle of straw", Mark's forty-plus "immediately", John's verb/noun pattern). Two mechanical notes short of a revise: the double-hyphen dash is used as the default connector throughout, and pronouns for Jesus are capitalized ("Him", "His") against the rest of the site's lowercase convention. "For serious readers" in the SEO line flatters a little.

page:client/src/pages/tools/ChurchHealth.notes: Sharp and often true ("the budget is a confession"; "If that terrifies you, the problem is not their readiness. It is your control"), but it runs entirely on the older gait the voice standard now ranks below developed paragraphs: aphoristic antithesis stacked line after line ("Confirmation is comfortable. Formation is costly. Formation is the task."; "Depth produces partnership. Breadth produces tourism."; "They are not performers. They are pastoral theologians with instruments.") and corporate leadership vocabulary the standard names as avoid ("leadership pipeline", "deployed", "develop the people who execute it", "one-page leadership development plan"). A pastor writing to pastors never once says "we"; every indictment is "your church". The lowest band handles the pastor well: "naming it is the first step" and a visible path to outside help.

page:client/src/pages/tools/ConflictGuid.notes: Crisis handling is exemplary: the safety notice ("that is not a conflict to resolve. It is a situation to get safe from") and the Domestic Violence Hotline sit before any step, and the betrayal track says plainly "Do not skip professional help." One stock line to cut: "Clarity is kindness" is the Brené Brown slogan. The "not X. It is Y." construction is the default rhythm of nearly every warning ("is not a conversation. It is a hostage negotiation"; "is not stewardship. It is control"; "is not virtue. It is a pattern"), which the standard lists as a tic once its work is done; thin a third of them. Otherwise the voice is pastoral and precise.

page:client/src/pages/tools/DeepBibleCom.notes: The scholarship is careful and steelmanned (the satan as "prosecuting attorney, not a fallen angel — at least in this text"), but several fixable failures: "God moved into the neighborhood" is Eugene Peterson's Message rendering of John 1:14 used without attribution; "Jeremiah 29:11 ... is the most quoted verse in America" is unverifiable as stated; "The emotional authenticity makes it the model" uses a forbidden word; the SEO promise "PhD-level depth made accessible" and the hero's "No pastor required. No seminary required" are hype hooks, the latter an odd line for a pastor's platform. The paraphrase blocks run on fragment stacks and em-dashes ("Not command. Not demand. Speak."; "Not guilty. Period.") as the default gait rather than at hinges. "And here is the scandal:" is signposting.

"Are you in."), which reads as a copy error in a sentence meant to be sent to a neighbor; "reproducing plan" is repeated as jargon in SEO, hero, and body.

page:client/src/pages/tools/LifeAudit.ts.notes: The interpretation and next-step copy runs on the fragment-stack gait the voice standard retires: "This is not a moral failing. It is a diagnostic." / "Not eloquent prayer. Honest prayer." / "Not tomorrow. Today." / "Depth is not found. It is built" recur across nearly every block until the move is a tic, and several closers are hype ("That sentence changes the trajectory," "It will tell you everything," "would change everything else"). "You are doing the work that most people avoid" is therapy-speak, and the Strained band diagnoses the reader with a condition they never named: "The good news is that you took this assessment, which means the denial is breaking." The SEO description promises "eight life areas" and lists seven. The crisis band does keep a path to help visible ("a counselor, a pastor, a trusted friend... Do not try to do this alone").

Earn it." / "Not as punishment -- as a declaration" / "This is not a verdict -- it is a diagnosis. And a diagnosis is a gift"), plus corporate filler ("This is not a crisis -- it is an opportunity") and superlative hype ("the most courageous thing a married person can do," "the difference between a good marriage and a great one"). As wonder.", and corporate phrasing like "relational infrastructure." The voice that says it will never lift is not telling you the truth"), alludes to self-harm without specifics, and puts 988 and named counseling paths first. The recovery-step copy needs work: unsourced statistics stated as fact ("the single greatest predictor of pastoral failure," "the leading cause of forced pastoral exits," "the most common and most devastating form of pastoral burnout," "movement is the only thing that breaks the neurological loop"), hype ("Healthy board relationships are ministry gold... Many pastors would trade their salary for what you have"), and the fragment tic ("Gently. Firmly. Without choosing a side. That is the prophetic task."). "Give yourself permission to feel nothing in response to congregational need" should be reworded; it reads as counsel to go numb. A chapter-a-day matched to the calendar date is a modern devotional habit, not a documented practice of the church across centuries; "There are thirty-one chapters for a reason" implies a design that is not there. Drop the pedigree and the page is honest and good: "Open your Bible to Proverbs {n} and read the whole chapter slowly. These are only the door."

page:client/src/pages/tools/QuoteLibrary.notes: Short, honest utility copy that tells the reader where every line came from and sends them back to it: "Every quote comes from a longer argument. Read the full essays." "The lines that stop you mid-scroll" is a social-feed framing that a stricter pass could trade for something quieter, but it describes the product accurately and is not bait.

page:client/src/pages/tools/RuleOfLife.t.notes: Full thoughts, the traditional trellis image used rather than decorated, and no demand register: "A rule of life is not a list of demands to fail at. It is a trellis... Choose what you can actually sustain. Begin small." "A short rule kept beats a long rule abandoned" is a verdict earned by the sentence before it. The book bridge stays an invitation.

One goal: Scripture that lives in you, not just on a screen." The SEO description claims "proven techniques" with nothing behind the word. Verses are NIV throughout (Philippians 4:6-7, Proverbs 3:5-6, Galatians 2:20, etc.) with a ScriptureNote present; keep the translation named. No altar call." Case intros were not in the extract; the frame copy ships.

page:client/src/pages/tools/TheologyGlos.notes: Scholarship is mostly solid (Nicaea 325/381, Chalcedon 451, Trent, Athanasius's 367 letter, Barth's Nein! 1934, Benedictus Deus 1336 all check), the contested entries steelman both sides, and the register is calm. Two citation fixes: the Supersessionism entry credits "Justin Martyr, Adversus Judaeos," but Justin's work is the Dialogue with Trypho and Adversus Judaeos belongs to Tertullian and the later genre; and the Propitiation entry says Romans 3:25 calls Christ "the hilasmos" when Romans uses hilasterion (hilasmos is 1 John). The "Why It Matters" lines lean on a superlative tic ("the most neglected metaphor," "the most uncomfortable word," "the most misunderstood," "the most persistent temptation," "the most counter-cultural claim Christianity makes," "the most radical claim in the history of ethics") that should be thinned.

page:client/src/pages/tools/VerseFinder..notes: Hero copy is honest about what the tool shows and sends the reader to context: "The line shown is the part that bears on the topic — tap any reference to read the whole passage in context." The verse texts are NIV (Isaiah 41:10, Lamentations 3:22-23, Romans 8:38-39, etc.), not the site's ESV default; no ScriptureNote appears in the extract, so confirm the translation is named on the page. page:client/src/pages/tools/WhichLens.ts.notes: The lens verdicts do the hard things right: fair before sharp on both the Flag and the Cause "with the same grief," the Rearview honored before it is refused, no sneer at the Marketplace reader. The revision is a biography check, not a voice fix: "the man who built this site carried the same lens for years," "preached the edited version for years and was discipled by men who did the same," "has flinched the same way — softened a hard word because the room would have gone cold," and "it worked on the man writing these words too" are specific claims about James's life beyond the four known facts. Confirm each with him or generalize the self-implication to "we."

page:client/src/pages/tools/WisdomFinder.notes: The hero speaks plainly to the seeker ("Tell us what you are struggling with, in your own words") and the integrity line is exactly right: "The verse text below is shortened to the line in view. Tap any reference to read the whole passage." One mechanical fix in the empty state, where a colon is missing: "in a word or two, anxiety, anger, money..." reads as a run-on.

library:client/public/family-reading-pla.notes: The voice holds across all 115 fields: plain, unhurried, one scene and one honest question per day, self-implicating where it counts ([3].days[5].prompt: "that includes all of us at this table"), and the questions honor real trouble without preaching ([0].days[7].prompt: "what storm is scaring your family right now"). Two accuracy/mechanics slips keep it from shipping as-is. [1].days[4].prompt adds a detail Genesis 6–7 does not contain: "Noah builds a huge boat because God told him to, while everyone laughs" — the laughing is folk tradition, not text, and this library tells families to read straight off the page; cut the clause. [1].days[25].prompt has a missing possessive ("God shuts the lions mouths"). Lesser: [0].days[25].prompt imports Luke's "sweating" into a Mark reading (Mark 14 has no sweat), and [0].days[14].prompt and [2].days[18].prompt embed questions without a question mark. The uniform "Scene. Ask X." shape is a functional format for a prompt library, not the AI symmetry the standard warns against, and passes.

library:client/public/family-seasonal.js.notes: This is the strongest family copy in the set — advent[6].reflection ("Some families this December are missing someone at the table. The promise is not that the dark is fake"), holyWeek[3] ("every one of us has chosen something small over someone who loved us"), holyWeek[5] ("Let today feel heavy. It was.") honor pain, implicate the writer, and end with weight. Three fixable failures: advent[18].reflection lifts Eugene Peterson's Message rendering of John 1:14 verbatim and unattributed ("He moved into the neighborhood") — attribute it or rephrase, since the standard forbids passing another writer's sentence off as ours; advent[21].reflection lands on the stock AI turn the standard names ("Some things you just hold and let sink in"); advent[4].reflection puts a car in ancient Judah ("the kind of place people drove past"). Pattern note for the editor rather than a failure: the "Not X. Y." antithesis recurs as the hinge of roughly a third of the reflections (advent[0], [6], [10], [18], [20]); read one per night it works, read together it becomes a tic — thin it. Structural, not voice: advent[1], [3], [7], [9]–[12], [14], [16], [22], [23] and holyWeek[3], [5] ship without a question and/or prayer, which reads as inconsistency to a parent using it nightly.
